title: Ad Astra - How much does your situation influence how much you to like or dislike a film?

commenti.body:
Around it's release a joke that popped up in a lot of discussions of it was that your enjoyment of the film was directly proportional to how complicated the relationship you have with your dad is. 


I do think there's some truth in it and with your general point about your situation affecting your enjoyment. Slower films with a few fumbles are going to be far more influenced by how much it resonates with your personal situation effectively papering over the cracks. Contrast to something like Aftersun which got universal acclaim among people that will be OK with a slow plotless film which despite bring deeply personal your situation doesn't have a big impact (beyond making some people find it *really* brilliant) on whether you like it at all because it's so well executed.


For what it's worth I enjoyed Ad Astra and have a complicated relationship with my dad.
To me it correlated more with how lonely and powerless I feel. I don't have a complicated relationship with my dad at all (he's dead), but these feelings kicked so hard.

The atmosphere building was excellent in that movie, definitely made an impression. I was personally hoping for a more “Heart of Darkness” approach to traveling further and further from the sun, but I get them wanting to prioritize the father-son relationship instead. 

That being said, god dammit I wish they did more research or consulted better with science experts. There was so much wrong with it on that front, and they weren’t nit picky mistakes but outright sloppy ones. The fact that the special effects were so great with such glaring mistakes made it all the more painful. If they got it right while emphasizing the descent into madness angle more it would probably be one of my favorite films.

Situation and unconscious bias affect significantly.

With a wrong mindset, you can have expectations about something the movie never try to do.

Or if you hate the franchise, the genre or any element of the movie due to outside information, mostly likely you're gonna end up ignoring most of the good things and just focus on the bad things. That lead to a bad time.
Yeah, don’t like my dad or men in general, so I was rooting for space.

The movie got taken away from James Gray in post. Some of the changes were good, but some weren’t. A lot of the sloppy mistakes came from that. 

Looking carefully, a bunch of the egregious stuff (like the nonsense at the opening briefing) is done through ADR lines. Like how it cuts from John Ortiz saying a line to briefing documents where he continues talking, but now it’s ADR that makes no scientific sense.

One change I didn’t like was adding sound to the moon buggy chase. James Gray originally intended for that entire sequence to be completely silence which would’ve been fantastic. 

Hopefully a miracle happens and we get a Director’s Cut like we did for The Yards.

Two things I’m not clear about are when Ruth Negga’s character >!was changed from the main character’s half-sister to a random helpful person!< and whether the original ending >!where he finds his father already dead on the Lima Project and never gets closure!< was ever shot.

I definitely consider my mood before hitting the play button on anything. There have been times where I've watched a film, or a TV season, etc, and, when asked "What'd you think of <x>?", I've said "It didn't really grab me. But it seemed like it was something I'd normally enjoy, so..I don't know that I was in the proper mindset for it at the time." It doesn't happen frequently or anything, but occurred enough times for me to take a step back and avoid force-feeding myself something just because it's on my current to-do list. Anymore, I keep relatively long lists for my pursuits so that I can fumble around a bit until something clicks in that, not only do I want to check it out - I'm \*excited\* in that moment to do it NOW.

A good example in my experience, albeit from a different medium, was Red Dead Redemption 2. I knew it was gonna be a banger, everyone was raving about it upon its release, but I decided to wait until it was the right time for me, where I was interested in getting into something that might require 50-100 hours of being on a roll with it. 

So yeah - for me, it's almost unfair to the product to take it in when you're not feeling the moment, be it due to the subject matter, the length, or if you're just feeling plain anhedonic.  Or it's unfair to yourself, I suppose, really - you can end up "wasting" the opportunity to enjoy something to its fullest, something that might join the ranks of your lifetime greats, simply because..you chose to watch it on an airplane, or while some real-life responsibility was nagging at your mind, preventing you from anything close to immersion.

The theory of life you explained is basically just the idea of nature vs nurture but the emphasis is on nurture. And someone’s long term and short term experience is always relevant to their response to something. 

For example, I lost my dad shortly before Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close came out. Instead of finding that movie charming or just harmless, I was legitimately angry at how it portrayed grief.

On the flip side, I saw Bottoms in a theater full of people and everyone was cracking up. It made the experience of the film a lot more fun and energized than it would be if I watched it on my phone while in bed. 

Personal and external context definitely matter. That’s why repeat viewings are usually good. Because they help us cut through the initial context.

>"It didn't really grab me. But it seemed like it was something I'd normally enjoy, so..I don't know that I was in the proper mindset for it at the time." 

Totally! This is the principle I adhere to and I hate when people are casual about like browsing phones or watching a cinema-copy(generally downloaded from a torrent), but I reserve my expressing my displeasure as I don't want to be a social outcast :P  
Weekend afternoons with a proper sleep the night before, door closed, a cup of tea is the perfect set-up for me.

I wanted to enjoy RDR2 but it was slow paced for the time I could devote to it because of my situation in life(late 30s, lot's of responsibilities and competing hobbies). But my god I love artistic progress games have gone through over the days of Mario and Contra which were the first non-portable video games I played a lot.

> nature vs nurture

Yeah, I almost wrote that. I have come to a conclusion that we value nature or than nurture through my experiences in life but opposite is true. I was born gifted and never had to work to achieve great things. But in my 30s did it hit me like a wrecking ball! If I was forced/taught to value discipline more than the output(grades) it would have been easier.

Another instance- I am a parent to an 8 year old who's not my biological son. And people tell me he has many of my peculiarities. And I am very peculiar! And I am not talking about mannerisms but he picked up more integral traits like curiosity, talking about nature of time, infinity, taste etc. BTW same people tell me when will I have my own biological son(it's a thing in my culture) and I roll my eyes.

>For what it's worth I enjoyed Ad Astra and have a complicated relationship with my dad.

I am parent to a kid who's biological dad was mostly absent. It pained to feel that maybe one day he will grow up and watch this film and yearn for his absent father similarly.

You’re good on Gravity. It’s just so stressful. When it becomes about just her, it’s not awful, but it reminded of La Voix Humaine. I totally don’t judge your view. Often, films with extended periods with only one actor are extremely stressful. Stress Films are a one and done for me, even with multiple actors, like Requiem for a Dream and Schindler’s List. Directors like Hitchcock and Tarantino are masters at finding ways to take a stressful and add excitement so that you’re intrigued. Gravity is a doom and gloom film.

I thought Ad Astra was a bit of a modern classic because it was brave enough to face truly modern questions: what do we do when society falls apart and we find ourselves alone in the universe with no where else to escape. Where does our meaning come from?
